description: Atomic structure, alpha, beta, and gamma radiation, nuclear equations, half-life, contamination vs irradiation.
content_html:
Atomic Structure and Isotopes

Every atom has a nucleus made of protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons, which carry negative charge, occupy energy levels around the nucleus. The number of protons is the atomic number and defines which element the atom is. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. Nuclear notation is written as \(^A_Z X\), where \(A\) is the mass number (protons + neutrons) and \(Z\) is the atomic number. For example, carbon-12 (\(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 protons and 6 neutrons; carbon-14 (\(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

Key Fact

Isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons. Unstable isotopes have nuclei that decay spontaneously, emitting ionising radiation. Radioactive decay is random and cannot be predicted for any individual nucleus.

Types of Ionising Radiation

Unstable nuclei emit three main types of ionising radiation:

• Alpha (\(\alpha\)) particles — a helium nucleus (\(^4_2\text{He}\)): 2 protons + 2 neutrons. Strongly ionising because of their large charge and mass. Weakly penetrating: stopped by a single sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.
• Beta (\(\beta\)) particles — a high-speed electron produced when a neutron converts into a proton inside the nucleus. Moderately ionising and penetrating. Stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
• Gamma (\(\gamma\)) rays — high-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus. Weakly ionising but highly penetrating: only significantly reduced by several centimetres of lead or metres of concrete.

Increasing ionising power: \(\gamma\) < \(\beta\) < \(\alpha\). Increasing penetrating power: \(\alpha\) < \(\beta\) < \(\gamma\). There is a trade-off — the more ionising a particle is, the more energy it deposits quickly and the less it penetrates.

In any nuclear equation, the mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance on both sides.

Alpha decay: nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Mass number decreases by 4; atomic number decreases by 2.

$$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$

Beta decay: a neutron converts to a proton. Mass number unchanged; atomic number increases by 1.

$$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$$

Gamma emission: no change to mass number or atomic number. Gamma is often emitted alongside alpha or beta decay as the nucleus releases excess energy.

Key Fact

Alpha decay: mass number −4, atomic number −2. Beta decay: mass number unchanged, atomic number +1. Gamma emission: no change to either. Numbers must balance on both sides of a nuclear equation.

Ionisation and Detecting Radiation

Ionising radiation knocks electrons from atoms, creating ions. This damages living cells by breaking chemical bonds and can mutate DNA, potentially causing cancer. Alpha particles are the most ionising, which is why swallowed or inhaled alpha sources are the most biologically dangerous, even though they are stopped by skin externally.

In the laboratory, a Geiger–Müller (GM) tube connected to a counter detects ionising radiation by measuring the electrical pulses produced when radiation enters the tube. The activity of a radioactive source is measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 nuclear decay per second. Always measure and subtract the background count rate (radiation present without the source) before recording results.

Half-Life

Half-life is the time taken for the number of unstable (undecayed) nuclei in a sample to halve — or equivalently for the activity to halve. Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous: you cannot predict when any individual nucleus will decay, but you can predict the average rate of decay for a large sample.

After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives, a quarter remain. After three, an eighth. For example, if a sample has an initial activity of 800 Bq and its half-life is 3 hours, after 9 hours (3 half-lives): \(800 \rightarrow 400 \rightarrow 200 \rightarrow 100\) Bq.

The fraction of radioactive nuclei remaining after \(n\) half-lives is given by: $$\text{fraction remaining} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$ For example, after 5 half-lives: \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5 = \frac{1}{32}\). If the original count rate was 6400 Bq, after 5 half-lives it would be \(6400 \times \frac{1}{32} = 200\) Bq.

Background radiation is always present in the environment. Natural sources include radon gas from rocks (the largest source of exposure in the UK), cosmic rays from space, and radioactive materials in food and building materials. Artificial sources include medical procedures (such as X-rays) and discharges from the nuclear industry, though these contribute a much smaller proportion of the total.

Because background radiation varies from place to place and over time, you must take a background count before any laboratory measurement of a radioactive source, then subtract it from your readings to get the corrected count rate from the source alone.

Contamination and Irradiation

It is essential to distinguish between two different hazards:

Contamination occurs when radioactive material is deposited on or inside a person or object. The source continues to emit radiation in close contact with tissues. This is generally considered more dangerous than irradiation because the exposure is continuous and cannot be stopped by simply moving away. It is removed by washing or decontamination procedures.

Irradiation occurs when a person is exposed to radiation from an external source. The person does not themselves become radioactive. Once the source is removed, the irradiation stops. The risk depends on the type of radiation, dose received and duration of exposure.
exam_tip_html: Nuclear equation questions require all mass numbers and atomic numbers to balance — check both sides before moving on. For half-life calculations, work methodically: find how many half-lives fit into the total time, then halve the activity that many times. For extended-response questions on the risks of radiation, use the terms contamination and irradiation precisely — examiners reward clear distinction between the two. Remember: alpha is the most ionising but least penetrating; gamma is the least ionising but most penetrating.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous. Alpha particles (helium nucleus), beta particles (high-speed electron) and gamma rays (EM radiation) differ in ionising power, penetrating power and how nuclear equations change.
  • Half-life is the time for activity to halve. After \(n\) half-lives, \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\) of the original nuclei remain.
  • Contamination (radioactive material on/in the body) is more dangerous than irradiation (external exposure) because it provides continuous, close-range exposure that cannot be stopped by distance.

practice_questions.text: State the change in mass number and atomic number when a nucleus undergoes beta decay.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: mass number unchanged. 1 mark: atomic number increases by 1.

practice_questions.text:
Complete the nuclear equation for the alpha decay of radium-226 (atomic number 88):
²²⁶₈₈Ra → ? + ⁴₂He
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct mass number 222. 1 mark: correct atomic number 86 (radon). Full answer: ²²²₈₆Rn.

practice_questions.text: A radioactive source has an initial count rate of 1200 counts per minute and a half-life of 8 hours. Calculate the count rate after 24 hours.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: identifies number of half-lives = 24 ÷ 8 = 3. 1 mark: shows repeated halving: 1200 → 600 → 300 → 150. 1 mark: correct answer 150. 1 mark: correct unit (counts per minute).

practice_questions.text: Explain why contamination by an alpha-emitting source is considered particularly hazardous, even though alpha particles are stopped by skin.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that if an alpha source enters the body (inhaled or ingested), the alpha particles are in direct contact with internal tissues; alpha is the most ionising type of radiation so causes maximum damage to cells and DNA at close range; continuous exposure cannot be reduced simply by distance since the source is inside the body. Secure: states alpha causes most ionisation close up, and contamination means the source stays inside the body. Developing: states alpha is dangerous when inside the body without explaining why ionisation causes more damage internally. Emerging: mentions contamination and alpha without distinguishing internal vs external exposure.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following correctly states the penetrating power of the three types of ionising radiation in order from least to most penetrating?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: Alpha, beta, gamma. Distractors: Gamma, beta, alpha; Beta, alpha, gamma; Alpha, gamma, beta.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of carbon-14 dating as a method of determining the age of ancient organic materials. Include a discussion of its strengths and limitations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that carbon-14 is taken in by living organisms; after death, the proportion of carbon-14 decreases as it decays; by measuring the remaining count rate and using the known half-life of carbon-14, the age can be calculated; strengths include accuracy for samples up to several tens of thousands of years; limitations include that it cannot be used for materials older than this range (activity too low to measure reliably), requires knowledge of the original carbon-14 ratio, and cannot be used for non-organic materials. Secure: explains mechanism and gives one strength and one limitation. Developing: describes basic principle but limitations are vague. Emerging: mentions carbon-14 and age without mechanism.

knowledge_checks.q: What type of particle is emitted during alpha decay?
A sample has an activity of 400 Bq and a half-life of 2 hours. What is its activity after 6 hours?
Radioactive decay is described as _____ because you cannot predict when any individual nucleus will decay.
During beta decay, the atomic number of the nucleus _____ by 1 while the mass number stays the same.
Match each radiation type to its penetrating ability.
right: Stopped by a few mm of aluminium
Only reduced by thick lead or concrete
Stopped by paper or a few cm of air

flashcard_questions.a: An atom with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons from another atom of the same element.

flashcard_questions.q: What particles make up an alpha particle?
flashcard_questions.a: 2 protons and 2 neutrons (identical to a helium nucleus).

flashcard_questions.q: What is emitted during beta decay?
flashcard_questions.a: A high-speed electron from the nucleus when a neutron converts to a proton.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by paper?
Which type of radiation is most ionising and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Alpha radiation is most ionising because it has a large charge and mass, so it interacts strongly with surrounding matter.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of radiation is most penetrating?

flashcard_questions.a: The time for half the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay (or for activity to halve).

flashcard_questions.q: A source has activity 640 Bq and half-life 5 hours. What is its activity after 15 hours?
In alpha decay, how do mass number and atomic number change?
flashcard_questions.a: Mass number decreases by 4; atomic number decreases by 2.
When radioactive material is deposited on or inside a person or object, causing ongoing radiation exposure.
Exposure to radiation from an external source; the person does not become radioactive.
Low-level ionising radiation present in the environment at all times from natural and artificial sources.

flashcard_questions.q: What unit measures the activity of a radioactive source?
flashcard_questions.a: Becquerels (Bq) — 1 Bq equals 1 decay per second.

glossary_terms.definition: Positively charged particles found in the nucleus of an atom; the number of protons defines the element.
Neutral particles found in the nucleus of an atom with approximately the same mass as protons.
Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A particle made of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus), emitted from an unstable nucleus. Highly ionising; stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron converts to a proton. Moderately ionising; stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from an unstable nucleus. Weakly ionising but highly penetrating; only significantly reduced by thick lead or concrete.
The time taken for half of the unstable nuclei in a radioactive sample to decay, or for the activity to halve.
When a radioactive material is deposited on or inside a person or object, providing an ongoing source of radiation exposure.
Exposure to ionising radiation from an external source; the person does not become radioactive and exposure stops when the source is removed.
Low-level ionising radiation present in the environment at all times, from natural sources such as radon gas and cosmic rays, and from artificial sources.
